{{Short description|Quantum physics-based metaheuristic for optimization problems}}
{{Other uses|Annealing (disambiguation)}}
{{Technical|date=January 2022}}
{{Use American English|date=January 2019}}

'''Quantum annealing''' ('''QA''') is an optimization process for finding the [[global minimum]] of a given [[objective function]] over a given set of candidate solutions (candidate states), by a process using [[quantum fluctuation]]s.<ref name="Chakrabarti89">{{Cite journal |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.39.11828 |pmid=9948016 |title=Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model in a transverse field: Absence of replica symmetry breaking due to quantum fluctuations |journal=[[Physical Review B]] |volume=39 |issue=16 |pages=11828–11832 |year=1989 |last1=Ray |first1=P. |last2=Chakrabarti |first2=B. K. |last3=Chakrabarti |first3=A. |bibcode=1989PhRvB..3911828R}}</ref> Quantum annealing is used mainly for problems where the search space is discrete ([[combinatorial optimization]] problems) with many [[local minimum|local minima]], such as finding the [[ground state]] of a [[spin glass]] or solving [[Quadratic unconstrained binary optimization|QUBO]] problems, which can encode a wide range of problems like [[Maximum cut|Max-Cut]], [[graph coloring]], [[Satisfiability|SAT]] or the [[traveling salesman problem]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lucas |first1=Andrew |date=2014 |title=Ising formulations of many NP problems |journal=Frontiers in Physics |volume=2 |page=5|doi=10.3389/fphy.2014.00005 |doi-access=free |arxiv=1302.5843 |bibcode=2014FrP.....2....5L }}</ref> The term "quantum annealing" was first proposed in 1988 by B. Apolloni, N. Cesa Bianchi and D. De Falco as a quantum-inspired classical algorithm.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Apolloni |first1=Bruno |last2=Cesa-Bianchi |first2=Nicolo |last3=De Falco |first3=Diego |title=A numerical implementation of quantum annealing |publisher=Stochastic Processes, Physics and Geometry, Proceedings of the Ascona-Locarno Conference |date=July 1988 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/250309136}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Apolloni |first1=Bruno |last2=Carvalho |first2=Maria C. |last3=De Falco |first3=Diego |date=1989 |title=Quantum stochastic optimization |journal=[[Stochastic Processes and Their Applications|Stoc. Proc. Appl.]] |volume=33 |issue=2 |pages=233–244 |doi=10.1016/0304-4149(89)90040-9 |doi-access=free}}</ref> It was formulated in its present form by T. Kadowaki and H. Nishimori ([[:ja:西森秀稔|ja]]) in 1998,<ref name="Kadowaki98">{{cite journal |last1=Kadowaki |first1=T. |last2=Nishimori |first2=H. |year=1998 |title=Quantum annealing in the transverse Ising model |url=http://pre.aps.org/abstract/PRE/v58/i5/p5355_1 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130811142150/http://pre.aps.org/abstract/PRE/v58/i5/p5355_1 |archive-date=2013-08-11 |journal=[[Phys. Rev. E]] |volume=58 |issue=5 |page=5355 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevE.58.5355 |bibcode=1998PhRvE..58.5355K |arxiv=cond-mat/9804280 |s2cid=36114913}}</ref> though an imaginary-time variant without quantum coherence had been discussed by A. B. Finnila, M. A. Gomez, C. Sebenik and J. D. Doll in 1994.<ref name="Finilla94">{{cite journal |last1=Finnila |first1=A. B. |last2=Gomez |first2=M. A. |last3=Sebenik |first3=C. |last4=Stenson |first4=C. |last5=Doll |first5=J. D. |year=1994 |title=Quantum annealing: A new method for minimizing multidimensional functions |journal=[[Chemical Physics Letters]] |volume=219 |issue=5–6 |pages=343–348 |arxiv=chem-ph/9404003 |bibcode=1994CPL...219..343F |doi=10.1016/0009-2614(94)00117-0 |s2cid=97302385}}</ref>

Quantum annealing starts from a quantum-mechanical superposition of all possible states (candidate states) with equal weights. Then the system evolves following the time-dependent [[Schrödinger equation]], a natural quantum-mechanical evolution of physical systems. The amplitudes of all candidate states keep changing, realizing a quantum parallelism, according to the time-dependent strength of the transverse field, which causes [[Quantum tunnelling|quantum tunneling]] between states or essentially tunneling through peaks. If the rate of change of the transverse field is slow enough, the system stays close to the ground state of the instantaneous [[Hamiltonian (quantum mechanics)|Hamiltonian]] (also see [[adiabatic quantum computation]]).<ref name="Farhi01">{{cite journal |last1=Farhi |first1=E. |last2=Goldstone |first2=J. |last3=Gutmann |first3=S. |last4=Lapan |first4=J. |last5=Ludgren |first5=A. |last6=Preda |first6=D. |year=2001 |title=A Quantum adiabatic evolution algorithm applied to random instances of an NP-Complete problem |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1057726 |journal=[[Science (journal)|Science]] |volume=292 |issue=5516 |pages=472–5 |doi=10.1126/science.1057726 |pmid=11313487 |arxiv=quant-ph/0104129 |bibcode=2001Sci...292..472F |s2cid=10132718}}</ref> If the rate of change of the transverse field is accelerated, the system may leave the ground state temporarily but produce a higher likelihood of concluding in the ground state of the final problem Hamiltonian, i.e., [[Diabatic representation|Diabatic]] quantum computation.<ref name="Crosson14">{{cite arXiv | eprint=1401.7320 | last1=Crosson | first1=Elizabeth | last2=Farhi | first2=Edward | author3=Cedric Yen-Yu Lin | last4=Lin | first4=Han-Hsuan | last5=Shor | first5=Peter | title=Different Strategies for Optimization Using the Quantum Adiabatic Algorithm | year=2014 | class=quant-ph }}</ref><ref name="Muthukrishnan15">{{cite arXiv | eprint=1505.01249 | last1=Muthukrishnan | first1=Siddharth | last2=Albash | first2=Tameem | last3=Lidar | first3=Daniel A. | title=When Diabatic Trumps Adiabatic in Quantum Optimization | year=2015 | class=quant-ph }}</ref> The transverse field is finally switched off, and the system is expected to have reached the ground state of the classical [[Ising model]] of [[spin glass]] that corresponds to the solution to the original optimization problem. A foundational study of the transverse Ising spin glass model was made by B. K. Chakrabarti in 1981.<ref name="chakrabarti81">{{cite journal |title=Critical behavior of the Ising spin-glass models in a transverse field |year=1981 |last1=Chakrabarti|first1= B.K.|journal=Physical Review B |volume=24 |issue=7 |article-number=4062 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.24.4062 |bibcode=1981PhRvB..24.4062C }}</ref> An experimental demonstration of the success of quantum annealing for random magnets was reported immediately after the initial theoretical proposal.<ref name="Brooke99">{{cite journal |last1=Brooke |first1=J. |last2=Bitko |first2=D. |last3=Rosenbaum |first3=T. F. |last4=Aeppli |first4=G. |year=1999 |title=Quantum annealing of a disordered magnet |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.284.5415.779 |journal=Science |volume=284 |issue=5415 |pages=779–81 |doi=10.1126/science.284.5415.779 |pmid=10221904 |arxiv=cond-mat/0105238 |bibcode=1999Sci...284..779B |s2cid=37564720}}</ref> Quantum annealing has also been proven to provide a fast [[Grover's algorithm|Grover]] oracle for the square-root speedup in solving many [[NP-completeness|NP-complete problems]].<ref name="sinitsyn23">{{cite journal |title=Topologically protected Grover's oracle for the partition problem|year=2023 |last1=Sinitsyn |first1=N. |last2=Yan |first2=B.|journal=Physical Review A |volume=108 |issue=2 |article-number=022412 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevA.108.022412 |arxiv=2304.10488 |bibcode=2023PhRvA.108b2412S |s2cid=258236417 }}</ref>

==Comparison to simulated annealing==
Quantum annealing can be compared to [[simulated annealing]], whose "temperature" parameter plays a similar role to quantum annealing's tunneling field strength. In simulated annealing, the temperature determines the probability of moving to a state of higher "energy" from a single current state. In quantum annealing, the strength of transverse field determines the quantum-mechanical probability to change the amplitudes of all states in parallel. Analytical<ref name="Morita08">{{Cite journal |doi=10.1063/1.2995837 |title=Mathematical foundation of quantum annealing |journal=[[Journal of Mathematical Physics]] |volume=49 |issue=12 |page=125210 |year=2008 |last1=Morita |first1=Satoshi |last2=Nishimori |first2=Hidetoshi |bibcode=2008JMP....49l5210M |arxiv=0806.1859 |s2cid=13992889}}</ref> and numerical<ref name="Santoro06">{{cite journal |url=http://iopscience.iop.org/0305-4470/39/36/R01 |title=Optimization using quantum mechanics: quantum annealing through adiabatic evolution |first1=Giuseppe E. |last1=Santoro |first2=Erio |last2=Tosatti |name-list-style=amp |date=18 August 2006 |journal=[[Journal of Physics A]] |volume=39 |number=36|pages=R393–R431 |doi=10.1088/0305-4470/39/36/R01 |bibcode=2006JPhA...39R.393S |s2cid=116931586 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> evidence suggests that quantum annealing outperforms simulated annealing under certain conditions (see Heim et al<ref name="Heim15">{{cite journal |last1=Heim |first1=B. |last2=Rønnow |first2=T. F. |last3=Isakov |first3=S. V. |last4=Troyer |first4=M. |year=2015 |title=Quantum versus classical annealing of Ising spin glasses |journal=Science |volume=348 |issue=6231 |pages=215–217 |doi=10.1126/science.aaa4170 |pmid=25765071 |arxiv=1411.5693 |bibcode=2015Sci...348..215H |doi-access=free}}</ref> and see Yan and Sinitsyn<ref name="SolvableQA">{{cite journal |last1=Yan |first1=B. |last2=Sinitsyn |first2=N. A. |year=2022 |title=Analytical solution for nonadiabatic quantum annealing to arbitrary Ising spin Hamiltonian |journal=Nature Communications |volume=13 |issue=1 |page=2212 |doi=10.1038/s41467-022-29887-0  |doi-access=free|pmid=35468917 |pmc=9038765 |arxiv=2110.12354|bibcode=2022NatCo..13.2212Y |s2cid=248389790 }}</ref> for a fully solvable model of quantum annealing to arbitrary target Hamiltonian and comparison of different computation approaches).

== Quantum mechanics: analogy and advantage ==
[[File:Quantum Annealing Analogy.svg|thumb|upright=1.5|alt=Simple analogy describing the difference between Simulated Annealing and Quantum Annealing.|Quantum Annealing (blue line) efficiently traverses energy landscapes by leveraging quantum tunneling to find the global minimum. Quantum annealing offers a significant performance advantage over Simulated Annealing (magenta line), unlocking the potential to solve massive optimization problems previously thought to be impossible.]]
The tunneling field is basically a kinetic energy term that does not commute with the classical potential energy part of the original glass. The whole process can be simulated in a computer using [[quantum Monte Carlo]] (or other stochastic technique), and thus obtain a heuristic algorithm for finding the ground state of the classical glass.

In the case of annealing a purely mathematical ''objective function'', one may consider the variables in the problem to be classical degrees of freedom, and the cost functions to be the potential energy function ([[Classical Hamiltonian quaternions|classical Hamiltonian]]). Then a suitable term consisting of non-commuting variable(s) (i.e. variables that have non-zero commutator with the variables of the original mathematical problem) has to be introduced artificially in the Hamiltonian to play the role of the tunneling field (kinetic part). Then one may carry out the simulation with the quantum Hamiltonian thus constructed (the original function + non-commuting part) just as described above. Here, there is a choice in selecting the non-commuting term and the efficiency of annealing may depend on that.

It has been demonstrated experimentally as well as theoretically, that quantum annealing can outperform thermal annealing (simulated annealing) in certain cases, especially where the potential energy (cost) landscape consists of very high but thin barriers surrounding shallow local minima.<ref name="local minima">{{Cite web |url=http://mathonline.wikidot.com/local-maxima-and-minima-and-absolute-maxima-and-minima |title=Local Maxima and Minima, and, Absolute Maxima and Minima |website=Mathonline}}</ref> Since thermal transition probabilities (proportional to <math>e^{-\frac{\Delta}{k_B T}}</math>, with <math>T</math> the temperature and <math>k_B</math> the [[Boltzmann constant]]) depend only on the height <math>\Delta</math> of the barriers, for very high barriers, it is extremely difficult for thermal fluctuations to get the system out from such local minima. However, as argued earlier in 1989 by Ray, Chakrabarti & Chakrabarti,<ref name="Chakrabarti89" /> the quantum tunneling probability through the same barrier (considered in isolation) depends not only on the height <math>\Delta</math> of the barrier, but also on its width <math>w</math> and is approximately given by <math>e^{-\frac{\sqrt{\Delta} w}{\Gamma}}</math>, where <math>\Gamma</math> is the tunneling field.<ref name="Das05">{{cite journal |url=http://pre.aps.org/abstract/PRE/v72/i2/e026701 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20140113104409/http://pre.aps.org/abstract/PRE/v72/i2/e026701 |archive-date=2014-01-13 |title=Quantum annealing in a kinetically constrained system |first1=A. |last1=Das |first2=B. K. |last2=Chakrabarti |first3=R. B. |last3=Stinchcombe |name-list-style=amp |date=2005 |journal=[[Phys. Rev. E]] |volume=72 |number=2 |article-number=026701 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevE.72.026701|pmid=16196745 |arxiv=cond-mat/0502167 |bibcode=2005PhRvE..72b6701D |s2cid=16466621 }}</ref> This additional handle through the width <math>w</math>, in presence of quantum tunneling, can be of major help: If the barriers are thin enough (i.e. <math>w \ll \sqrt{\Delta}</math>), quantum fluctuations can surely bring the system out of the shallow local minima. For an <math>N</math>-spin glass, the barrier height <math>\Delta</math> becomes of order <math>N</math>. For constant value of <math>w</math> one gets <math>\tau</math> proportional to <math>e^{\sqrt{N}}</math> for the annealing time (instead of <math>\tau</math> proportional to <math>e^N</math> for thermal annealing), while <math>\tau</math> can even become <math>N</math>-independent for cases where <math>w </math> decreases as <math>1/\sqrt{N}</math>.<ref name="Mukherjee15">See e.g., {{cite journal |title=Multivariable Optimization: Quantum Annealing & Computation |first1=S. |last1=Mukherjee |first2=B. K. |last2=Chakrabarti |name-list-style=amp |date=2015 |journal=[[Eur. Phys. J.]] |volume=224 |number=1 |pages=17–24 |doi=10.1140/epjst/e2015-02339-y |arxiv=1408.3262|bibcode=2015EPJST.224...17M |s2cid=118525494 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |first1=A. |last1=Das |first2=B. K. |last2=Chakrabarti |title=Quantum Annealing and Analog Quantum Computation |journal=[[Reviews of Modern Physics|Rev. Mod. Phys.]] |volume=80 |issue=3 |pages=1061–1081 |year=2008 |doi=10.1103/RevModPhys.80.1061 |bibcode=2008RvMP...80.1061D |arxiv=0801.2193 |s2cid=14255125}}</ref>

It is speculated that in a [[quantum computer]], such simulations would be much more efficient and exact than that done in a classical computer, because it can perform the tunneling directly, rather than needing to add it by hand. Moreover, it may be able to do this without the tight error controls needed to harness the [[quantum entanglement]] used in more traditional quantum algorithms. Some confirmation of this is found in exactly solvable models.<ref name='Li-18prl'>{{cite journal |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.121.190601 |pmid=30468584 |title=Quantum annealing and thermalization: insights from integrability |first1=F. |last1=Li |first2=V. Y. |last2=Chernyak |first3=N. A. |last3=Sinitsyn |name-list-style=amp |journal=[[Physical Review Letters]] |volume=121 |issue=19 |year=2018 |article-number=190601 |bibcode=2018arXiv180400371L |arxiv=1804.00371 |s2cid=53594139}}</ref><ref name="Yan-18prl">{{cite journal |title=Analytical solution for nonadiabatic quantum annealing to arbitrary Ising spin Hamiltonian |first1=B. |last1=Yan |first2=N. A. |last2=Sinitsyn |journal=Nature Communications |year=2022 |volume=13 |issue=1 |page=2212 |doi=10.1038/s41467-022-29887-0  |doi-access=free|pmid=35468917 |pmc=9038765 |arxiv=2110.12354|bibcode=2022NatCo..13.2212Y |s2cid=248389790 }}</ref>

Timeline of ideas related to quantum annealing in Ising spin glasses:
*1981 Ising spin glass in transverse (tunneling) field was proposed and studied;<ref name="chakrabarti81" />
*1989 Idea was presented that quantum fluctuations could help explore rugged energy landscapes of the classical Ising spin glasses by escaping from local minima (having tall but thin barriers) using tunneling;<ref name="Chakrabarti89" />
*1998 Formulation of quantum annealing and numerical test demonstrating its advantages in Ising glass systems;<ref name="Kadowaki98" />
*1999 First experimental demonstration of quantum annealing in LiHoYF Ising glass magnets;<ref name="Aeppli99">{{cite journal |title=Quantum Annealing of a Disordered Magnet |first1=J. |last1=Brooke |first2=D. |last2=Bitko |first3=T. F. |last3=Rosenbaum |first4=G. |last4=Aeppli |name-list-style=amp |date=30 April 1999 |journal=Science |volume=284 |issue=5415 |pages=779–781 |doi=10.1126/science.284.5415.779 |pmid=10221904 |bibcode=1999Sci...284..779B |s2cid=37564720 |url=https://authors.library.caltech.edu/46977/ |arxiv=cond-mat/0105238 |archive-date=22 May 2022 |access-date=3 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220522081135/https://authors.library.caltech.edu/46977/ }}</ref>
*2011 Superconducting-circuit quantum annealing machine built and marketed by D-Wave Systems.<ref name="Johnson11">{{cite journal |first1=M. W. |last1=Johnson |first2=M. H. S. |last2=Amin |first3=S. |last3=Gildert |display-authors=etal |year=2011 |title=Quantum annealing with manufactured spins |url=http://www.nature.com/nature/journal/v473/n7346/abs/nature10012.html |journal=Nature |volume=473 |issue=7346 |pages=194–8 |doi=10.1038/nature10012 |bibcode=2011Natur.473..194J |pmid=21562559 |s2cid=205224761|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==D-Wave implementations==
{{Further|D-Wave Systems#Computer systems|D-Wave Two}}

[[File:DWave 128chip.jpg |thumb |Photograph of a chip constructed by [[D-Wave Systems]], mounted and wire-bonded in a sample holder. The [[D-Wave One]]'s processor is designed to use 128 [[superconducting]] logic elements that exhibit controllable and tunable coupling to perform operations.]]

In 2011, [[D-Wave Systems]] announced the first commercial quantum annealer on the market by the name D-Wave One and published a paper in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' on its performance.<ref name="Johnson11"/> The company claims this system uses a 128 [[qubit]] processor chipset.<ref name="DWave11">{{cite web |title=Learning to program the D-Wave One |url=http://dwave.wordpress.com/2011/05/11/learning-to-program-the-d-wave-one/ |website=D-Wave Systems blog |access-date=11 May 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110723043401/http://dwave.wordpress.com/2011/05/11/learning-to-program-the-d-wave-one/ |archive-date=July 23, 2011}}</ref> On May 25, 2011, D-Wave announced that [[Lockheed Martin]] Corporation entered into an agreement to purchase a D-Wave One system.<ref name="DWavesys11">{{cite web |url=http://www.dwavesys.com/en/pressreleases.html#lm_2011 |title=D-Wave Systems sells its first Quantum Computing System to Lockheed Martin Corporation |website=D-Wave |access-date=2011-05-30 |date=2011-05-25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110723052206/http://www.dwavesys.com/en/pressreleases.html |archive-date=July 23, 2011}}</ref> On October 28, 2011 [[University of Southern California]]'s (USC) [[Information Sciences Institute]] took delivery of Lockheed's D-Wave One.

In May 2013, it was announced that a consortium of [[Google]], [[NASA Ames]] and the non-profit [[Universities Space Research Association]] purchased an adiabatic quantum computer from D-Wave Systems with 512 qubits.<ref name="Jones13">{{cite journal |last1=Jones |first1=N. |year=2013 |title=Google and NASA snap up quantum computer |url=http://www.nature.com/news/google-and-nasa-snap-up-quantum-computer-1.12999 |journal=Nature News |doi=10.1038/nature.2013.12999 |s2cid=57405432|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Smelyanskiy12">{{cite arXiv | eprint=1204.2821 | last1=Smelyanskiy | first1=Vadim N. | last2=Rieffel | first2=Eleanor G. | last3=Knysh | first3=Sergey I. | last4=Williams | first4=Colin P. | last5=Johnson | first5=Mark W. | last6=Thom | first6=Murray C. | last7=Macready | first7=William G. | last8=Pudenz | first8=Kristen L. | title=A Near-Term Quantum Computing Approach for Hard Computational Problems in Space Exploration | year=2012 | class=quant-ph }}</ref> An extensive study of its performance as quantum annealer, compared to some classical annealing algorithms, is available.<ref name="Boixo14">{{cite journal |last1=Boixo |first1=S. |last2=Rønnow |first2=T. F. |last3=Isakov |first3=S. V. |last4=Wang |first4=Z. |last5=Wecker |first5=D. |last6=Lidar |first6=D. A. |last7=Martinis |first7=J. M. |last8=Troyer |first8=M. |year=2014 |title=Evidence for quantum annealing with more than one hundred qubits |url=http://www.nature.com/nphys/journal/v10/n3/full/nphys2900.html |journal=[[Nature Physics]] |volume=10 |issue=3 |pages=218–224 |doi=10.1038/nphys2900 |bibcode=2014NatPh..10..218B |arxiv=1304.4595 |s2cid=8031023}}</ref>

In June 2014, D-Wave announced a new quantum applications ecosystem with computational finance firm [[1QB Information Technologies]] (1QBit) and cancer research group DNA-SEQ to focus on solving real-world problems with quantum hardware.<ref name="DWavesys14">{{cite web |title=D-Wave Systems Building Quantum Application Ecosystem, Announces Partnerships with DNA-SEQ Alliance and 1QBit |url=http://dwavesys.com/press-releases/d-wave-systems-building-quantum-application-ecosystem-announces-partnerships-dna-seq |website=D-Wave Systems |access-date=22 June 2014 |archive-date=31 December 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191231185125/http://www.dwavesys.com/press-releases/d-wave-systems-building-quantum-application-ecosystem-announces-partnerships-dna-seq }}</ref> As the first company dedicated to producing software applications for commercially available quantum computers, 1QBit's research and development arm has focused on D-Wave's quantum annealing processors and has demonstrated that these processors are suitable for solving real-world applications.<ref name="1qbit14">{{cite web |title=1QBit Research |url=http://1qbit.com/research.html |website=1QBit |access-date=22 June 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140619053448/http://www.1qbit.com/research.html |archive-date=19 June 2014 }}</ref>

With demonstrations of [[Quantum entanglement|entanglement]] published,<ref name="prx14">{{cite journal |first1=T. |last1=Lanting |first2=A. J. |last2=Przybysz |first3=A. Yu. |last3=Smirnov |first4=F. M. |last4=Spedalieri |display-authors=etal |title=Entanglement in a quantum annealing processor |journal=[[Physical Review X]] |date=2014-05-29 |volume=4 |issue=2 |article-number=021041 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevX.4.021041 |arxiv=1401.3500 |bibcode=2014PhRvX...4b1041L |s2cid=19235104}}</ref> the question of whether or not the D-Wave machine can demonstrate [[Quantum supremacy|quantum speedup]] over all classical computers remains unanswered. A study published in [[Science (magazine)|Science]] in June 2014, described as "likely the most thorough and precise study that has been done on the performance of the D-Wave machine"<ref name="Harv14">Helmut Katzgraber, quoted in {{Harv|Cho|2014}}.</ref> and "the fairest comparison yet", attempted to define and measure quantum speedup. Several definitions were put forward as some may be unverifiable by empirical tests, while others, though falsified, would nonetheless allow for the existence of performance advantages. The study found that the D-Wave chip "produced no quantum speedup" and did not rule out the possibility in future tests.<ref name="Cho14">{{Cite journal |first1=Adrian |last1=Cho |date=20 June 2014 |title=Quantum or not, controversial computer yields no speedup |journal=Science |volume=344 |issue=6190 |pages=1330–1331 |doi=10.1126/science.344.6190.1330 |pmid=24948715 |bibcode=2014Sci...344.1330C|doi-access=free }}</ref> The researchers, led by Matthias Troyer at the [[ETH Zurich|Swiss Federal Institute of Technology]], found "no quantum speedup" across the entire range of their tests, and only inconclusive results when looking at subsets of the tests. Their work illustrated "the subtle nature of the quantum speedup question". Further work<ref name="Amin15">{{cite journal | arxiv=1503.04216 | doi=10.1103/PhysRevA.92.052323 | title=Searching for quantum speedup in quasistatic quantum annealers | year=2015 | last1=Amin | first1=Mohammad H. | journal=Physical Review A | volume=92 | issue=5 | article-number=052323 | bibcode=2015PhRvA..92e2323A | s2cid=66770023 }}</ref> has advanced understanding of these test metrics and their reliance on equilibrated systems, thereby missing any signatures of advantage due to quantum dynamics.

There are many open questions regarding quantum speedup. The ETH reference in the previous section is just for one class of benchmark problems. Potentially there may be other classes of problems where quantum speedup might occur. Researchers at Google, LANL, USC, Texas A&M, and D-Wave are working to find such problem classes.<ref name="Steiger15">{{Cite book |editor1-first=David A. |editor1-last=Huckridge |editor2-first=Reinhard |editor2-last=Ebert |editor3-first=Mark T. |editor3-last=Gruneisen |editor4-first=Miloslav |editor4-last=Dusek |editor5-first=John G. |editor5-last=Rarity |first1=Damian |last1=Steiger |first2=Bettina |last2=Heim |first3=Troels |last3=Rønnow |first4=Matthias |last4=Troyer |title=Electro-Optical and Infrared Systems: Technology and Applications XII; and Quantum Information Science and Technology |chapter=Performance of quantum annealing hardware |date=October 22, 2015 |volume=9648 |page=964816 |doi=10.1117/12.2202661 |bibcode=2015SPIE.9648E..16S |s2cid=57916974}}</ref>

In December 2015, Google announced that the [[D-Wave 2X]] outperforms both [[simulated annealing]] and [[Quantum Monte Carlo]] by up to a factor of 100,000,000 on a set of hard optimization problems.<ref name="Google15">{{Cite web |title=When can Quantum Annealing win? |url=http://googleresearch.blogspot.com/2015/12/when-can-quantum-annealing-win.html |website=Research Blog |date=8 December 2015 |access-date=2016-01-21}}</ref>

D-Wave's architecture differs from traditional quantum computers. It is not known to be polynomially equivalent to a [[universal quantum computer]] and, in particular, cannot execute [[Shor's algorithm]] because Shor's algorithm requires precise gate operations and quantum Fourier transforms which are currently unavailable in quantum annealing architectures.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Johnson |first1=M. W. |last2=Amin |first2=M. H. S. |last3=Gildert |first3=S. |last4=Lanting |first4=T. |last5=Hamze |first5=F. |last6=Dickson |first6=N. |last7=Harris |first7=R. |last8=Berkley |first8=A. J. |last9=Johansson |first9=J. |last10=Bunyk |first10=P. |last11=Chapple |first11=E. M. |last12=Enderud |first12=C. |last13=Hilton |first13=J. P. |last14=Karimi |first14=K. |last15=Ladizinsky |first15=E. |date=May 2011 |title=Quantum annealing with manufactured spins |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/nature10012 |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=473 |issue=7346 |pages=194–198 |doi=10.1038/nature10012 |pmid=21562559 |bibcode=2011Natur.473..194J |issn=1476-4687|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Shor's algorithm requires a universal quantum computer. During the Qubits 2021 conference held by D-Wave, it was announced<ref>{{Cite web |author=D-Wave Systems |date=2021-10-05 |title=D-Wave's Next-Generation Roadmap: Bringing Clarity to Practical Quantum Computing |url=https://dwave.medium.com/d-waves-next-generation-roadmap-bringing-clarity-to-practical-quantum-computing-192b3275c73d |access-date=2021-11-12 |website=Medium |language=en}}</ref> that the company is developing their first universal quantum computers, capable of running Shor's algorithm in addition to other gate-model algorithms such as [[Quantum optimization algorithms|QAOA]] and [[Variational quantum eigensolver|VQE]].

"A cross-disciplinary introduction to quantum annealing-based algorithms"<ref name="VenegasAndraca2018">{{cite journal |last1=Venegas-Andraca |first1=Salvador E. |last2=Cruz-Santos |first2=William |last3=McGeoch |first3=Catherine |last4=Lanzagorta |first4=Marco |year=2018 |title=A cross-disciplinary introduction to quantum annealing-based algorithms |arxiv=1803.03372 |journal=[[Contemporary Physics]] |volume=59 |issue=2 |pages=174–196 |doi=10.1080/00107514.2018.1450720 |bibcode=2018ConPh..59..174V |s2cid=118974781}}</ref> presents an introduction to combinatorial optimization ([[NP-hardness|NP-hard]]) problems, the general structure of quantum annealing-based algorithms and two examples of this kind of algorithms for solving instances of the max-SAT (maximum satisfiable problem) and Minimum Multicut problems, together with an overview of the quantum annealing systems manufactured by D-Wave Systems. Hybrid quantum-classic algorithms for large-scale discrete-continuous optimization problems were reported to illustrate the [[Quantum supremacy|quantum advantage]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ajagekar |first1=Akshay |last2=Humble |first2=Travis |last3=You |first3=Fengqi |date=2020-01-04 |title=Quantum computing based hybrid solution strategies for large-scale discrete-continuous optimization problems |journal=[[Computers & Chemical Engineering]] |language=en |volume=132 |article-number=106630 |doi=10.1016/j.compchemeng.2019.106630 |arxiv=1910.13045 |issn=0098-1354 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Wierzbiński23">{{cite journal |last1=Wierzbiński|first1=M.|last2=Falo-Roget|first2=J. |last3=Crimi |first3=A.  |year=2023 |title=Community detection in brain connectomes with hybrid quantum computing |journal=Scientific Reports|volume=13 |issue=1 |page=3446 |doi=10.1038/s41598-023-30579-y |doi-access=free|pmid=36859591 |pmc=9977923 |bibcode=2023NatSR..13.3446W |s2cid=257236235 }}</ref>
